expectedText:
MANDATORY CHILD CUSTODY MEDIATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Alex Doe · Jane Doe

DECLARATION -- SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet addresses the mediation of custody and visitation disputes concerning Alex Doe under California Family Code Chapter 11 (Mediation of Custody and Visitation Issues, commencing with Section 3160), in a matter involving Jane Doe and John Doe pending in Los Angeles County. It describes the circumstances under which this mediation is required, the purposes the mediation statute itself states, the confidentiality of communications made in mediation, the mediator's availability, qualifications, and duties, the statutory distinction between a mediator who may submit a custody or visitation recommendation to the court and the separate, narrower confidential mediation program under which a mediator may not, and a domestic-violence-specific mediation procedure that is separate from the pre-mediation notice California law requires under Family Code section 3044(h).

WHEN MEDIATION IS REQUIRED, AND ITS TIMING
Under California law, if it appears on the face of a petition, application, or other pleading to obtain or modify a temporary or permanent custody or visitation order that custody, visitation, or both are contested, the court is required to set the contested issues for mediation. Where a matter is set for mediation under this chapter, the statute requires that the mediation be set before or concurrent with the setting of the matter for hearing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) If it appears on the face of a petition, application, or other pleading to obtain or modify a temporary or permanent custody or visitation order that custody, visitation, or both are contested, the court shall set the contested issues for mediation."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3170(a) (California Legislative Information text), the mandatory mediation trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3170.)
  "If a matter is set for mediation pursuant to this chapter, the mediation shall be set before or concurrent with the setting of the matter for hearing."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3175 (California Legislative Information text), the requirement that mediation be set before or concurrent with the hearing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3175.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two independent sections of the same statutory chapter (Family Code Chapter 11, Mediation of Custody and Visitation Issues, Sections 3160-3188): section 3170(a), in Article 2 (Availability of Mediation, Sections 3170-3173), and section 3175, in Article 3 (Mediation Proceedings, Sections 3175-3188). It does not restate section 3170(b)'s separate domestic-violence-protocol provision (addressed in a separate clause of this document), section 3171's parallel mediation trigger for stepparent or grandparent visitation petitions, section 3172's rule that mediation may not be denied because paternity is contested, or section 3173's separate procedure for mediating a dispute over an existing custody or visitation order. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, mandatory pre-hearing (or concurrent-with-hearing) mediation mechanism -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody or visitation matter; whether, when, and on what trigger mediation is required varies by state.

THE STATUTE'S OWN STATEMENT OF MEDIATION'S PURPOSE
California's mediation-of-custody-and-visitation statute states its own purposes: to reduce acrimony that may exist between the parties; to develop an agreement assuring the child close and continuing contact with both parents that is in the child's best interest, consistent with the statute's general custody provisions; and to effect a settlement of visitation rights that is in the child's best interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The purposes of a mediation proceeding are as follows: (a) To reduce acrimony that may exist between the parties. (b) To develop an agreement assuring the child close and continuing contact with both parents that is in the best interest of the child, consistent with Sections 3011 and 3020. (c) To effect a settlement of the issue of visitation rights of all parties that is in the best interest of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3161 (California Legislative Information text), the statute's own statement of mediation's purposes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3161.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 3161), quoted in full as one contiguous provision covering its three lettered purposes; no additional independent source was found for this. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's own mediation statute says its purposes are -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific matter, and not a claim about how effectively mediation achieves these stated purposes in any specific case.

CONFIDENTIALITY OF MEDIATION COMMUNICATIONS
Under California law, mediation proceedings held under this chapter must be held in private and are confidential; communications from the parties to the mediator made in the proceeding, whether verbal or written, are official information within the meaning of Evidence Code section 1040. Where notice of mediation is given for the confidential mediation program under section 3188, that notice must itself state that all communications involving the mediator will be kept confidential between the mediator and the disputing parties.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Mediation proceedings pursuant to this chapter shall be held in private and shall be confidential. All communications, verbal or written, from the parties to the mediator made in the proceeding are official information within the meaning of Section 1040 of the Evidence Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3177 (California Legislative Information text), the general confidentiality rule for mediation communications (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3177.)
  "Notice of mediation pursuant to Section 3188 shall state that all communications involving the mediator shall be kept confidential between the mediator and the disputing parties."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3176(c) (California Legislative Information text), the requirement that notice under the section 3188 confidential mediation program disclose confidentiality (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3176.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two provisions of the same statutory chapter: section 3177 (the general confidentiality rule for mediation communications) and section 3176(c) (a notice-content requirement tied specifically to section 3188's confidential mediation program, addressed in a separate clause of this document). It does not independently analyze Evidence Code section 1040's 'official information' privilege itself, including any exceptions to that privilege, which is a separate code section this document does not verify. It also does not address how this statutory confidentiality interacts with a mediator's separate statutory authority to report an agreement, a recommendation, or unresolved issues to the court under sections 3183 through 3186, addressed in part in other clauses of this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific confidentiality rule -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific mediation.

THE MEDIATOR'S AVAILABILITY, QUALIFICATIONS, AND DUTIES
Under California law, each superior court must make a mediator available for these proceedings, and is not required to institute a family conciliation court to do so. The mediator may be a member of the professional staff of a family conciliation court, probation department, or mental health services agency, or any other person or agency the court designates, and must meet the minimum qualifications required of a counselor of conciliation. In the mediation proceeding itself, the mediator has the duty to assess the needs and interests of the child involved and is entitled to interview the child when the mediator considers the interview appropriate or necessary, and the mediator is required to use their best efforts to effect a settlement of the custody or visitation dispute that is in the child's best interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Each superior court shall make a mediator available. The court is not required to institute a family conciliation court in order to provide mediation services."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3160 (California Legislative Information text), the requirement that each superior court make a mediator available (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3160.)
  "(a) The mediator may be a member of the professional staff of a family conciliation court, probation department, or mental health services agency, or may be any other person or agency designated by the court. (b) The mediator shall meet the minimum qualifications required of a counselor of conciliation as provided in Section 1815."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3164 (California Legislative Information text), who may serve as mediator, and the minimum qualifications required (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3164.)
  "(a) In mediation proceedings pursuant to this chapter, the mediator has the duty to assess the needs and interests of the child involved in the controversy, and is entitled to interview the child when the mediator considers the interview appropriate or necessary. (b) The mediator shall use their best efforts to effect a settlement of the custody or visitation dispute that is in the best interest of the child, as provided in Section 3011."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3180 (California Legislative Information text), the mediator's duty to assess the child and the best-efforts settlement standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3180.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on three independent sections of the same statutory chapter: section 3160 (availability of a mediator), section 3164 (who may serve as mediator, and minimum qualifications), and section 3180 (the mediator's duty to assess the child and best-efforts standard). It does not address a mediator's authority to exclude counsel or a domestic violence support person from the proceeding (§ 3182), or the separate uniform standards of practice the Judicial Council is required to adopt for mediators (§ 3162), which this document does not independently cover or restate. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, checkable rules about who mediates these disputes and what the mediator is required to do -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific mediation, and not a description of any individual mediator's actual practice in a specific case.

RECOMMENDING MEDIATION AND THE SEPARATE CONFIDENTIAL MEDIATION PROGRAM
Under California law, except as provided in section 3188, a mediator may -- consistent with local court rules -- submit a recommendation to the court on custody or visitation, provided the mediator has first given the parties and their attorneys the recommendation in writing before the hearing; where a mediator is authorized to do this, the statute refers to the process as 'child custody recommending counseling' and to the mediator as a 'child custody recommending counselor.' Separately, a court selected by the Judicial Council may voluntarily adopt a confidential mediation program under which the mediator may not make a recommendation as to custody or visitation to anyone other than the disputing parties, except as the statute otherwise provides. That confidential-mediation-program section does not become operative until the Legislature appropriates funds sufficient to implement it, and by its own terms applies only in four or more superior courts the Judicial Council selects that already allow custody recommendations and have more than 1,000 family law case filings per year, though the Judicial Council may extend it to additional, smaller courts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as provided in Section 3188, the mediator may, consistent with local court rules, submit a recommendation to the court as to the custody of or visitation with the child, if the mediator has first provided the parties and their attorneys, including counsel for any minor children, with the recommendations in writing in advance of the hearing."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3183(a) (California Legislative Information text), the recommending mediation model, tied to local court rules (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3183.)
  "(a)Any court selected by the Judicial Council under subdivision (c) may voluntarily adopt a confidential mediation program that provides for all of the following: (1) The mediator may not make a recommendation as to custody or visitation to anyone other than the disputing parties, except as otherwise provided in this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3188(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the alternative confidential mediation program in which the mediator may not recommend to the court (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3188.)
  "(b) This section shall become operative upon the appropriation of funds in the annual Budget Act sufficient to implement this section. (c) This section shall apply only in four or more superior courts selected by the Judicial Council that currently allow a mediator to make custody recommendations to the court and have more than 1,000 family law case filings per year. The Judicial Council may also make this section applicable to additional superior courts that have fewer than 1,000 family law case filings per year."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3188(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), the funding-appropriation condition and the narrow scope of courts to which section 3188 applies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3188.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two independent sections of the same statutory chapter: section 3183(a) (the default, recommending model, whose availability the statute itself ties to 'local court rules') and section 3188 (the alternative confidential, non-recommending program). The statute itself does not use the shorthand terms 'recommending county' or 'non-recommending county' that California family-law practice commonly uses to describe this distinction -- those are practitioner and court-administration terms, not statutory language -- but sections 3183(a) and 3188 are the statutory provisions that produce the underlying distinction. Section 3188 is narrow on its own terms: it is conditioned on a legislative funding appropriation, and by its text applies only to a limited set of Judicial-Council-selected courts; this document does not verify whether that funding condition has been met, which courts (if any) currently operate under section 3188, or what any individual county's local court rule under section 3183(a) actually provides, since none of that is stated in the statutory text itself and was not independently researched here. This clause also does not restate section 3183(b) and (c) (a mediator's related authority to recommend a further investigation or a temporary restraining order) or section 3184 (a mediator's authority to recommend appointment of counsel for the child), which this document does not otherwise cover.

A DOMESTIC-VIOLENCE-SPECIFIC MEDIATION PROCEDURE, SEPARATE FROM THE SECTION 3044(H) NOTICE REQUIREMENT
Where mediation is required under this chapter and there has been a history of domestic violence between the parties, or a protective order is in effect, California law requires the mediator -- at the request of the party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury, or the party protected by the order -- to meet with the parties separately and at separate times; any intake form the family court services agency requires parties to complete before mediation begins must state that this separate-meeting option is available on request. Separately, domestic violence cases are required to be handled by Family Court Services under a written protocol the Judicial Council approves, and the Judicial Council is required to adopt guidelines for services -- other than mediation itself -- that courts or counties may offer parents who have been unable to resolve their disputes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) In a proceeding in which mediation is required pursuant to this chapter, where there has been a history of domestic violence between the parties or where a protective order as defined in Section 6218 is in effect, at the request of the party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury or protected by the order, the mediator appointed pursuant to this chapter shall meet with the parties separately and at separate times. (b) Any intake form that an agency charged with providing family court services requires the parties to complete before the commencement of mediation shall state that, if a party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury or a party protected by a protective order so requests, the mediator will meet with the parties separately and at separate times."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3181 (California Legislative Information text), the mediator's duty to meet with the parties separately and at separate times on request, and the related intake-form disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3181.)
  "Domestic violence cases shall be handled by Family Court Services in accordance with a separate written protocol approved by the Judicial Council. The Judicial Council shall adopt guidelines for services, other than services provided under this chapter, that courts or counties may offer to parents who have been unable to resolve their disputes. These services may include, but are not limited to, parent education programs, booklets, video recordings, or referrals to additional community resources."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3170(b) (California Legislative Information text), the separate written domestic-violence protocol and services-guidelines requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3170.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two independent sections of the same statutory chapter: section 3181 (the separate-meeting procedure and related intake-form disclosure) and section 3170(b) (the separate written protocol and services-guidelines requirement). It is deliberately distinct from, and does not restate, this project's Domestic Violence Custody Presumption document's clause on Family Code section 3044(h), which requires a court to inform the parties of section 3044 itself and give them a copy of it before custody mediation where a party has alleged the other perpetrated domestic violence within the meaning of that section -- a different statutory section, addressed to a different notice (of the section 3044 presumption, not of a right to be interviewed separately), and located outside this mediation chapter. This document does not verify the content of the separate written protocol section 3170(b) requires the Judicial Council to approve, or the guidelines it requires the Judicial Council to adopt, since neither is specified in the statutory text itself. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, mediation-chapter-internal domestic-violence procedures -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding, and not a claim that these are the only domestic-violence-related safeguards that could apply to a specific mediation.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT -- NOT A COURT ORDER OR DETERMINATION
I, Jane Doe, and I, John Doe, each acknowledge that I have reviewed this information sheet describing California's mediation-of-custody-and-visitation-disputes statute in connection with the matter concerning Alex Doe pending in Los Angeles County.

Executed on January 1, 2026.

☐ _________________________ Jane Doe, signature

☐ _________________________ John Doe, signature

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual filing or proceeding in the appropriate California superior court. It does not itself order mediation, does not determine whether a specific dispute concerning Alex Doe is contested within the meaning of Family Code section 3170, does not determine which mediation model -- recommending or confidential -- applies in Los Angeles County, and does not modify any existing custody or visitation order. Only the court, and the local court rules and Judicial Council programs applicable in Los Angeles County, determine how mediation actually proceeds in a specific matter.]

It is deliberately distinct from, and does not restate, this project's Domestic Violence Custody Presumption document's clause on Family Code section 3044(h), which requires a court to inform the parties of section 3044 itself and give them a copy of it before custody mediation where a party has alleged the other perpetrated domestic violence within the meaning of that section -- a different statutory section, addressed to a different notice (of the section 3044 presumption, not of a right to be interviewed separately), and located outside this mediation chapter. This document does not verify the content of the separate written protocol section 3170(b) requires the Judicial Council to approve, or the guidelines it requires the Judicial Council to adopt, since neither is specified in the statutory text itself. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, mediation-chapter-internal domestic-violence procedures -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding, and not a claim that these are the only domestic-violence-related safeguards that could apply to a specific mediation.
